name: daktilo
desc: Plays typewriter sounds every time you press a key
why: Turns every keystroke into a typewriter clack, a small but genuine audio-on-input toy that makes the terminal feel physical.

brief.what_it_is: daktilo is a small command-line program for Linux, Windows and macOS that plays a typewriter sound every time you press a key. It takes keyboard events as input and sends audio to your chosen output device. It ships with built-in sound presets (default, basic, musicbox, ducktilo, drumkit, spark) that can be stacked, and a TOML config file lets you map keys, matched by regex, to your own sound files with per-file volume, random or sequential playback, and randomized volume and tempo.
brief.why_it_exists: The author wants to recreate the feel of taking notes on a physical typewriter without owning one, for crafting emails or pranks. The README credits H. Arda Güler for the original idea and a first Python implementation.
brief.how_it_works: It listens for global key press and release events and plays the sound mapped to each key. Presets are arrays of key_config entries, each with an event, a regex for keys, and one or more audio files, with a strategy of random or sequential. Sound variation picks a random volume or playback-speed change within configured percentage limits on each keypress, and playing back at a different speed also shifts the pitch.

commands_seen.context: Runs daktilo with the musicbox preset, which plays random notes like a music box.
Stacks several presets at once; the README calls this 'orchestra'.
Sends playback to a specific output device.
Adds random tempo and volume variation to make the sounds more realistic.
Disables the easter eggs; the same can be set with no_surprises = true in the config file.
Writes the default configuration file to the current directory.
Installs from crates.io; needs Rust 1.70.0 or newer.
Installs from the Arch Linux official repositories.
Builds from a cloned repository; the binary ends up at target/release/daktilo.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install: on Linux, building with cargo needs ALSA and X input development packages (Arch: alsa-lib libxtst libxi; Alpine: alsa-lib-dev libxi-dev libxtst-dev; Debian/Ubuntu: libasound2-dev libxi-dev libxtst-dev). The minimum supported Rust version is 1.70.0. Alpine needs the testing repository enabled. MacPorts has a port (sudo port install daktilo). On macOS, the first run prompts for permissions, and you must enable Input Monitoring for your terminal app under Privacy and Security. Configuration can be passed with --config or DAKTILO_CONFIG, or placed at $XDG_CONFIG_HOME or $HOME/.config/daktilo.toml on Linux (equivalent locations on macOS and Windows). Running daktilo --init creates a default config file.
brief.standout: Unlike fixed-sound keyboard toys such as bucklespring, daktilo is data-driven: stackable presets, regex key matching, per-key sound files, and randomized pitch and volume per keypress. It also has easter eggs, which the README hides behind a spoiler warning.
brief.status: unknown. The fetched pages show no release or commit dates. The GitHub README has live release, crates.io, CI and release-workflow badges, and the project is packaged in Arch extra, Alpine edge, MacPorts and crates.io. Copyright is listed as 2023-2024. This suggests active upkeep, but I could not confirm recent activity.
brief.caveats: Wayland is not supported. The README marks it with an asterisk that points to the rdev limitation, and the Wayland box is unchecked. Supported platforms are X11 on Linux, Windows and macOS. macOS needs the Input Monitoring permission granted to the terminal before it will work. Building from source on Linux needs ALSA and X input dev packages. Easter eggs are on by default and can be turned off with --no-surprises or no_surprises = true. License is dual MIT or Apache-2.0 at your option.
